Chaos took over in the next few turns. Instead of taking the free piece with 6.Bxf5, which sets up a discovered attack on the queen via the d-file, you played 6.Nf3. Black retreated with 6...Qd6, creating a pin along the d-file, and once again 7.Bxf5 was available. Instead, you jumped in with 7.Nb5 and Black responded with 7...Qd7 before abruptly resigning.

review.turning_point: Black's blunder 5...Bf5 left a piece completely hanging on f5, though the game remained wildly unstable until Black resigned on move 7.
review.focus: Look for undefended pieces before making developing moves, such as capturing with 6.Bxf5 instead of playing 6.Nf3.

review.headline: A symmetrical French Defense derails after tactical oversights and a back-rank finish

sections.text: Out of the Exchange French, both sides developed smoothly until Black played 8...Nbd7, leaving the d5-pawn vulnerable. You missed the chance to grab it with 9.Nxd5 and instead opted for 9.Qd2. When Black gave you another opportunity with 9...Bg6, 10.Bd3 bypassed 10.Nxd5 once again, keeping the game balanced.

The game slipped in the middlegame when you played 17.N3h4, hanging your bishop to 17...Nxg5. Even after Black blundered with 23...h6, you missed 24.Nxe6 and instead played 24.Nxd6, a discovered attack on the e6-rook that still allowed Black to take your knight with 24...hxg5.
Down material, you pushed 26.cxd4, but it removed defense from your first rank. Black immediately punished it with 26...Qe1+ 27.Rxe1 Rxe1#.

review.turning_point: 17.N3h4 dropped a full minor piece to 17...Nxg5, handing Black a decisive advantage.
review.focus: Look for undefended pieces before choosing retreating or attacking moves, avoiding oversights like 17.N3h4.

review.headline: A chaotic bullet brawl turned around by a sharp tactical strike

sections.text: You fell into trouble early in the Scandinavian after pushing 4...e5 and 6...e4, which opened lines against your uncastled king and cost you a pawn. White traded down into a dominant endgame, but you stayed active by bringing your rooks to the center and hopping your knight to d4.
The game flipped when White played 19.Be3??, walking into a pin along the e-file. You punished it instantly with 19...f4!, winning a piece after 20.c3 fxe3 21.fxe3.

Instead of cashing in directly with 21...Rxe3, you retreated with 21...Nf5??, letting White push their central pawns. Still, you kept up the pressure, grabbed another pawn with 29...Nxd4, and took the win on time.

review.turning_point: White blundered with 19.Be3?? into the e-file pin, and your swift 19...f4! won the bishop to swing the evaluation from -2.5 to +4.4.
review.focus: Avoid overextending pawns in the opening when your king is still in the center, as seen with 6...e4?.

review.headline: A central breakthrough punishes an exposed king in a rapid bullet victory

sections.text: Your opponent opened with the Center Game, but after 5.e5, White overextended in the center far too early. You mobilized smoothly with 7...Nf6 and 8...O-O, lining up your major pieces against White's uncastled king.

When White blundered with 10.Nce4, you seized the initiative with 10...Nxe4, creating a discovered attack on White's g5-knight while blowing open the e-file. White was forced to surrender heavy material to prevent an immediate collapse, leaving you up a queen after 13...Bxe6.

Looking to finish the game, you played 15...Bc4+, unleashing a discovered check that also hung your queen to 15.Bg5. Fortunately, White missed the capture, blocking with 16.Be2, which pinned their own bishop and allowed 16...Qxe2#.

review.turning_point: White's central slip 10.Nce4 allowed your decisive strike 10...Nxe4, tearing open the e-file and netting White's queen.
review.focus: Even when delivering forcing checks, ensure your own pieces aren't left undefended, as 15...Bc4+ allowed White a clean capture on e7.

moves: c4 e5 Nc3 d6 e4 Nf6 Bd3 Be7 Nf3 O-O O-O Bg4 Be2

review.headline: A clean opening cut short

sections.text: You handled the Reversed Sicilian well from the start. After 1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 d6 3.e4 Nf6, you developed smoothly and prioritized king safety with 5...O-O. White played the awkward 4.Bd3, blocking their own d-pawn, which gave you easy equality.

You immediately clamped down on White's kingside piece play with 6...Bg4, forcing White to untangle by retreating with 7.Be2. The position was completely balanced and comfortable for Black, but the game unfortunately ended right here due to an early resignation.

review.turning_point: The game ended abruptly after 7.Be2, leaving the board in a dead-even position before any real fight could begin.
review.focus: Your opening play was solid up to 6...Bg4; just make sure to keep playing out balanced positions to see your middlegame plans through.
